StringWithMarkup.String: The enzyme systems in rat liver and lung responsible for the oxidative metabolism of hydrazine derivatives were studied to determine whether these enzymes, cytochrome p450 and monoamine oxidase, were responsible for metabolically activating hydrazines to carcinogenic/toxic metabolites. Cytochrome p450 preferentially oxidized the nitrogen to nitrogen bond of 1,2-disubstituted hydrazines and hydrazides, while monoamine oxidase oxidized the nitrogen to nitrogen bond of all the classes of hydrazine derivatives that were tested. StringWithMarkup.String: /CASE REPORTS/ A 55-year-old man with squamous-cell carcinoma of the left maxillary sinus presented with a 2-week history of rash, pruritus, progressive malaise, and jaundice. The patient had previously declined to undergo surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy. To treat his cancer, the patient had instead decided to use hydrazine sulfate he obtained through an alternative medicine Internet site. ...Two weeks before his presentation, he had discontinued /4 months/ use of hydrazine sulfate, 180 mg/d, after a bothersome rash developed. On physical examination, ... he was alert and conversant. There was no sinus tenderness or obvious facial asymmetry, and no masses were seen in the nasal passages. Inspection of the skin revealed a macular rash involving the chest and extremities, as well as prominent palmar erythema. Marked scleral icterus and jaundice were also evident. No hepatomegaly or other stigmata of liver disease were noted, and the remainder of the examination was normal. Laboratory studies revealed marked azotemia with a serum urea nitrogen level of 15.7 mmol/L (44 mg/dL) and a serum creatinine level of 450.8 umol/L (5.1 mg/dL). Results on liver function tests were as follows: serum aspartate aminotransferase level, 12.8 ukat/L (770 U/L); serum alanine aminotransferase level, 13 533.6 nkat/L (812 U/L); serum lactate dehydrogenase level, 9.8 ukat/L (586 U/L); serum bilirubin level, 738.7 umol/L (43.2 mg/dL); serum albumin level, 28 g/L; and prothrombin time, 19.5 seconds. A complete blood count revealed a leukocyte count of 19.2 x 109 cells/L, a hemoglobin level of 167 g/L, a hematocrit of 0.497, and a platelet count of 111 x 109 cells/L. Findings on electrocardiography, chest radiography, and abdominal ultrasonography were unremarkable. The patient was admitted to the hospital for hepatorenal failure associated with self-medication with hydrazine sulfate. Because hydrazine sulfate is a known antagonist of vitamin B6, this vitamin was administered intravenously.  On the third day of hospitalization, the patient developed hepatic encephalopathy that did not respond to lactulose. Progressive renal failure necessitated the initiation of hemodialysis, and coagulopathy persisted despite administration of vitamin K and several blood plasma transfusions. On the seventh hospital day, hematemesis occurred and prompted esophagoduodenoscopy, which revealed erosive esophagitis and diffuse hemorrhagic gastritis. No esophageal or gastric varices were detected. The patient never recovered from this episode despite aggressive treatment.

Hamsters were given hydrazine sulfate at 170, 340 and 510 mg/L in the drinking water for 2 years (average dose of 4.6, 8.3 and 10.3 mg hydrazine (free base)/kg bw over the 2-yr period), during which levels of methylation of DNA guanine in liver, kidney and lung, and histopathologic examinations of these tissues were carried out; dimethylnitrosamine, as a positive control, was administered at 10 mg/L in the drinking water (average dose of 1.1 mg/kg bw over the 4-month measurement period). Both 7-methylguanine and O6-methylguanine were readily detectable at 6 months exposure in hamsters given hydrazine or dimethylnitrosamine; in hydrazine-treated animals only trace amounts of these bases could be detected after 12 months exposure; these bases were again detected in liver DNA at exposure times of 18 and 24 months. Hepatocellular carcinomas were observed in hamsters treated at the highest dose of hydrazine sulfate after 78 weeks of exposure; the incidence of liver cancer was dose-related over the course of the experiment: 32% for hamsters exposed to 510 mg hydrazine sulfate/L, 12% for 340 mg/L and none at 170 mg/L. Hamsters given dimethylnitrosamine developed high levels of 7-methylguanine and even higher levels of O6-methylguanine and both liver cholangiocellular carcinomas (73% incidence), as reported before, and hepatocellular carcinomas (27% incidence), a new finding. These results demonstrate that hydrazine is a liver carcinogen in the hamster and provide information regarding the accumulation of DNA damage during the entire induction period for the carcinomas.

StringWithMarkup.String: Clastogenic activity was evaluated in 3 cultures of RL1 rat liver cells per dose, exposed for 22 hours to hydrazine sulfate at concentrations of 0, 25.0, 50.0, or 100.0 ug/ml of culture medium. Concentrations were chosen to be approximately 1/4, 1/2, and 1x the GI50 (concentration at which 50% growth inhibition is achieved). Both positive (7,12-dimethylbenzanthracene) and solvent (water) controls were used. No metabolic activation system was used. Cell division was arrested, and at least 290 metaphases from each test concentration were examined. Neither chromatid aberrations nor chromosome aberrations were increased significantly. The proportions of cells showing chromatid aberrations were 1.3%, 0.3%, 1.4%, and 1.1% at 0.0, 25.0, 50.0, and 100.0 ug/ml, respectively. The proportions of cells showing chromosome aberrations were 1.0%, 0.7%, 0.3%, and 0.3% at 0.0, 25.0, 50.0, and 100.0 ug/ml, respectively. Although the positive control compound induced chromatid aberrations in 8.4% of cells, only 1.0% showed chromosomal aberrations.
